Title: Development Stage Entities
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Start-ups once had to present inception-to-date information and label themselves 'development stage entities'. FASB removed the concept because it added cost without useful information — a young company follows the same GAAP as everyone else, with going-concern and risk disclosures doing the real work.
Recognition triggers:
• No separate recognition model: development-stage presentation requirements were removed by ASU 2014-15 (effective 2015).
• Start-up costs are expensed under ASC 720-15; going-concern evaluation under ASC 205-40.
• The source library holds only status content for this Topic.
Measurement:
Basis: Same as other entities
Initial: Apply the governing Topics.
Subsequent: No inception-to-date presentation.
Journal entries: Organization costs of a new property-management venture: DR Organization costs expense 40,000; CR Cash — operating 40,000
Audit traps:
Q: Must start-ups present inception-to-date results?
A: No — removed by ASU 2014-15.
Q: Where do start-up costs go?
A: Expensed as incurred (720-15).
Q: Is a going-concern evaluation still required?
A: Yes, under ASC 205-40 for every entity.

Title: Entertainment—Broadcasters
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: A TV station buys rights to air programs and earns ad revenue when they air. Program rights are assets recognized when the license period begins and the program is available, amortized as aired; FCC licenses are intangibles often with indefinite lives.
Recognition triggers:
• Recognize program rights as assets when the license period begins, the cost is known, the program is accepted and available for first showing (920-350).
• Amortize based on estimated number of showings or revenue pattern.
• FCC licenses: indefinite-lived intangibles tested for impairment.
Measurement:
Basis: Cost less amortization (program rights)
Initial: Initial: gross license fee (present value if significant financing).
Subsequent: Subsequent: amortize; impairment to net realizable value.
Journal entries: Recognize available program rights: DR Program rights 600,000; CR Program rights obligations 600,000
Audit traps:
Q: When are program rights recognized?
A: When the license period begins and all conditions are met — not at contract signing.
Q: Are FCC licenses amortized?
A: Typically not (indefinite life), but tested for impairment annually.
Q: How is advertising barter valued?
A: At fair value of goods/services received (606 noncash consideration).

Title: Entertainment—Cable Television
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Building a cable system takes years before subscribers fill it. During the prematurity period, costs are allocated between the portion serving current subscribers (expensed) and the portion for future subscribers (capitalized), so early losses aren't overstated nor profits flattered.
Recognition triggers:
• During prematurity, capitalize system costs and allocate certain costs between current and future subscribers (922-360).
• Initial hookup revenue recognized to the extent of direct selling costs; installation costs capitalized.
• Franchise costs capitalized and amortized.
Measurement:
Basis: Cost less depreciation
Initial: Allocate prematurity costs by subscriber fraction.
Subsequent: Depreciate plant over useful life.
Journal entries: Capitalize new-subscriber installation costs: DR Cable plant — subscriber installations 75,000; CR Accounts payable 75,000
Audit traps:
Q: What is the prematurity period?
A: The period before the system reaches break-even subscriber levels (usually ≤2 years) during which special cost allocation applies.
Q: Are reconnection costs capitalized?
A: No — expensed as incurred.
Q: Who applies this Topic?
A: Cable system operators; the source library contains only the Overall overview.

Title: Entertainment—Casinos
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Casinos hold customers' money as chips, promise progressive jackpots and give away free rooms and meals to gamblers. Outstanding chips are liabilities, progressive jackpots are accrued as the obligation builds (base jackpots only when won or unavoidable), and 'comps' are part of the gaming transaction under ASC 606.
Recognition triggers:
• Chips in customers' hands are a liability.
• Progressive jackpots accrued as the incremental amount builds; base jackpots not accrued if the casino can avoid payment by removing the machine.
• Complimentaries: allocate gaming revenue to comps by standalone selling price (606).
Measurement:
Basis: Net win (gaming revenue) under 606
Initial: Gaming revenue is net of payouts.
Subsequent: Update jackpot accruals as play occurs.
Journal entries: Accrue progressive jackpot increment: DR Gaming revenue (reduction) 30,000; CR Progressive jackpot liability 30,000
Audit traps:
Q: Are base jackpots accrued?
A: No, if the casino can avoid paying by removing the game; incremental progressive amounts are accrued.
Q: How are comps presented?
A: Gaming revenue is allocated to the comped goods/services (e.g., room revenue) under 606.
Q: Is gaming revenue gross wagers?
A: No — net win (wagers less payouts).

Title: Entertainment—Films
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: A film costs a fortune before earning anything, and its revenue arrives unevenly over years through theaters, streaming and licensing. So production costs are capitalized and amortized in proportion to revenue as it's earned (individual-film-forecast method), with impairment testing when the film won't recover its cost.
Recognition triggers:
• Report film costs as a separate asset (926-20-25-1); production overhead included; administrative/distribution costs excluded.
• Amortize using the individual-film-forecast method (current revenue ÷ ultimate revenue) or monetized with a group of films.
• Test for impairment when indicators exist (fair value, individually or in a film group).
• Participation costs accrued as revenue is recognized.
Measurement:
Basis: Capitalized cost less amortization and impairment
Initial: Accumulate production costs, including capitalized interest where applicable.
Subsequent: Amortize by revenue ratio; revise ultimate revenue estimates prospectively.
Journal entries: Amortize film costs: DR Film cost amortization 2,000,000; CR Film costs 2,000,000
Audit traps:
Q: Are marketing costs capitalized into film costs?
A: No — exploitation/marketing costs are expensed as incurred (advertising).
Q: How long can ultimate revenue be projected?
A: Generally up to 10 years from initial release (20 years for acquired libraries).
Q: Is impairment tested per film?
A: Individually, or at the film-group level when monetized as a group (e.g., streaming).

Title: Entertainment—Music
Review notes: Placeholder 'source note' trap replaced with a record-master capitalization trap.
First-principles truth: Record labels pay artists advances before knowing whether songs will sell. An advance is an asset only if past performance and current popularity make recovery from future royalties likely; otherwise it's expensed. Licensing revenue follows ASC 606's IP license guidance.
Recognition triggers:
• Capitalize artist advances when past performance and current popularity provide a sound basis for estimating recovery from future royalties.
• Cost of record masters is capitalized when recoverable from future sales.
• License revenue: ASC 606 IP licensing (functional IP at a point in time; sales-based royalties when sales occur).
Measurement:
Basis: Recoverable cost
Initial: Advances recorded as assets to the extent recoverable.
Subsequent: Charge to expense as royalties are earned; write down unrecoverable amounts.
Journal entries: Recoverable artist advance: DR Royalty advances 250,000; CR Cash — operating 250,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is every advance an asset?
A: No — only if recovery is reasonably assured based on past performance and popularity.
Q: How are sales-based royalties recognized by the licensor?
A: When the later of the sale or usage occurs and the performance obligation is satisfied (606 royalty exception).
Q: Is the cost of producing a record master capitalized?
A: Only the portion expected to be recovered from future sales, based on past performance and current popularity; the rest is expensed. The detailed rules sit in the music industry subtopics, which the source export does not include.

Title: Extractive Activities—Mining
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Mining is a long bet on what lies underground. Exploration spending before proven reserves exist is usually expensed because the payoff is uncertain; costs to develop a proven mine are capitalized; and waste removal once production starts (stripping) is a cost of the ore extracted in that period.
Recognition triggers:
• Exploration costs generally expensed until reserves are established; mineral rights acquisition capitalized.
• Development costs capitalized; depleted using units-of-production.
• Stripping costs incurred during the production phase are variable production costs included in inventory (930-330).
Measurement:
Basis: Cost; units-of-production depletion
Initial: Capitalized development costs and mineral rights at cost.
Subsequent: Deplete over proven and probable reserves.
Journal entries: Production-phase stripping costs: DR Inventory — ore 400,000; CR Accounts payable 400,000
Audit traps:
Q: Are production-phase stripping costs capitalized to PP&E?
A: No — they are inventory production costs.
Q: Is mineral exploration capitalized?
A: Generally expensed before reserves are established (differs from oil & gas successful-efforts rules).
Q: Depletion method?
A: Units-of-production based on reserves.

Title: Extractive Activities—Oil and Gas
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Drilling is a lottery: some wells hit, many are dry. Successful-efforts accounting capitalizes only the costs tied to discoveries and expenses dry holes; the full-cost method (SEC-permitted) capitalizes all exploration costs in a country-wide pool subject to a ceiling test. Either way, reserve quantities drive depletion and must be disclosed.
Recognition triggers:
• Successful efforts: capitalize acquisition and successful exploratory/development costs; expense geological & geophysical and dry-hole costs.
• Full cost (SEC rules, Reg S-X 4-10): capitalize all costs in cost centers, subject to a quarterly ceiling test.
• Supplementary reserve-quantity and standardized-measure disclosures (932-235).
Measurement:
Basis: Cost less depletion (units-of-production)
Initial: Capitalize per method.
Subsequent: Deplete using proved (developed) reserves; impair under 360 (SE) or ceiling test (FC).
Journal entries: Expense a dry exploratory well (successful efforts): DR Dry hole expense 3,200,000; CR Wells in progress 3,200,000
Audit traps:
Q: Which method expenses dry holes?
A: Successful efforts.
Q: What is the full-cost ceiling test?
A: Capitalized costs less related deferred taxes cannot exceed the present value (10%) of future net revenues from proved reserves plus certain other amounts.
Q: Are reserve disclosures audited?
A: Supplementary reserve information is required but typically unaudited (SEC registrants).

Title: Financial Services—Brokers and Dealers
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Broker-dealers hold customers' cash and securities and trade for their own account. Their inventory is marked to fair value, customer assets are segregated by regulation, and commissions are earned when trades execute — all to show whether the firm can meet obligations to customers.
Recognition triggers:
• Securities transactions recorded on trade date (940-320).
• Proprietary securities inventory at fair value with changes in earnings.
• Commission revenue recognized on trade date (606).
• Customer cash and securities segregated per SEC Rule 15c3-3.
Measurement:
Basis: Fair value (inventory); trade-date basis
Initial: Measure positions at fair value.
Subsequent: Remeasure each period; unrealized gains/losses in earnings.
Journal entries: Mark proprietary inventory to fair value: DR Securities owned, at fair value 120,000; CR Principal transactions revenue 120,000
Audit traps:
Q: Trade date or settlement date?
A: Trade date for regular-way trades.
Q: Are customer securities on the balance sheet?
A: Generally no — held in custody; customer cash payables and receivables are presented.
Q: Soft-dollar arrangements?
A: Research purchased with commissions must be accounted for and disclosed properly.

Title: Financial Services—Depository and Lending
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Banks turn deposits into loans. Their statements emphasize liquidity, credit quality and capital, so industry guidance governs how loans, deposits and regulatory capital are presented — while credit losses follow CECL (ASC 326) like everyone else.
Recognition triggers:
• Loans at amortized cost with CECL allowance (326-20); loan fees under 310-20.
• Deposits recognized as liabilities.
• SEC registrants follow Regulation S-X Article 9 presentation (942-10-S99).
Measurement:
Basis: Amortized cost (loans), face (deposits)
Initial: Loans net of deferred fees and allowance.
Subsequent: Update allowance each period.
Journal entries: Originate a commercial real estate loan: DR Loans receivable 5,000,000; CR Cash — operating 4,975,000; CR Deferred loan fees 25,000
Audit traps:
Q: Where are bank credit losses measured?
A: ASC 326 (CECL).
Q: Are origination fees revenue at closing?
A: No — deferred and amortized as yield adjustments.
Q: What is Article 9?
A: SEC Regulation S-X rules prescribing bank holding company statement formats and disclosures.

Title: Financial Services—Insurance
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: An insurer collects premiums today for promises that may come due years later. Premiums are earned over the coverage period, claims are reserved when insured events occur (including those incurred but not reported), and only successful acquisition costs are deferred. For long-duration contracts, LDTI requires updating assumptions so liabilities reflect current expectations.
Recognition triggers:
• Short-duration premiums: recognized over the contract period in proportion to protection provided.
• Claims liabilities (including IBNR) recognized when insured events occur.
• Deferred acquisition costs: only incremental direct costs of successful contract acquisition (944-30).
• Long-duration contracts (LDTI, ASU 2018-12): update cash-flow assumptions at least annually; discount rate from upper-medium-grade fixed-income yields (changes in OCI); market risk benefits at fair value.
Measurement:
Basis: Unearned premium; claims at ultimate cost; LFPB with current assumptions
Initial: Claims reserves at estimated ultimate cost (undiscounted for most short-duration).
Subsequent: Premium deficiency tests; DAC amortized on a constant-level basis (LDTI).
Journal entries: Earn one month of an annual property policy (insurer's side): DR Unearned premium reserve 100,000; CR Premiums earned 100,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is IBNR accrued?
A: Yes — incurred-but-not-reported claims are estimated and accrued.
Q: Which acquisition costs are deferrable?
A: Only incremental direct costs of successful contract acquisition (ASU 2010-26).
Q: Under LDTI, where do discount-rate changes go?
A: OCI for the liability for future policy benefits (instrument-specific credit risk for MRBs also OCI).

Title: Financial Services—Investment Companies
Review notes: Technical re-read of triggers, measurement, journal entries and traps; no changes needed.
First-principles truth: An investment company exists to earn returns from capital appreciation and income — not to operate what it owns. So its investments, including controlling stakes and real estate, are measured at fair value, and it does not consolidate operating investees. Investors then see NAV, the number they actually buy and redeem at.
Recognition triggers:
• Assess investment-company status at formation and reassess when facts change (946-10-25-1): fundamental characteristics (investment activities, returns from appreciation/income) and typical characteristics.
• Investments at fair value, including controlling interests in non-investment companies (no consolidation except of other investment companies or service providers).
• Report changes in net assets, financial highlights and schedules of investments.
Measurement:
Basis: Fair value; NAV
Initial: Initial: transaction price including transaction costs (then fair value).
Subsequent: Subsequent: fair value each reporting date with changes in net increase in net assets from operations.
Journal entries: Real estate fund records unrealized appreciation: DR Investments in real estate, at fair value 6,000,000; CR Net change in unrealized appreciation 6,000,000
Audit traps:
Q: Does a real estate fund depreciate its buildings?
A: Not if it is an investment company under 946 — properties are carried at fair value.
Q: Does a fund consolidate a majority-owned property LLC?
A: No — it measures the controlling interest at fair value (unless the investee is an investment company or provides services to the fund).
Q: Can an entity 'elect' investment-company accounting?
A: No — it must meet the fundamental characteristics; status is reassessed when circumstances change.

Title: Financial Services—Mortgage Banking
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: A mortgage banker originates loans to sell them, not to hold them. Loans held for sale are carried at the lower of cost or fair value (or fair value by election), and when loans are sold with servicing retained, the right to earn servicing fees is a separate asset.
Recognition triggers:
• Classify loans as held for sale or held for investment at origination; transfers at lower of cost or fair value.
• Loans held for sale: lower of cost or fair value (or fair value option).
• Mortgage servicing rights recognized when servicing is retained on sale (ASC 860-50).
Measurement:
Basis: Lower of cost or fair value / fair value
Initial: Held-for-sale loans measured in aggregate or individually.
Subsequent: Servicing rights amortized or at fair value by class.
Journal entries: Write down loans held for sale: DR Loss on loans held for sale 300,000; CR Valuation allowance — loans held for sale 300,000
Audit traps:
Q: Are held-for-sale loans subject to CECL?
A: No — they're at lower of cost or fair value (or FVO), outside the amortized-cost CECL model.
Q: Is an MSR recognized when servicing is retained?
A: Yes — at fair value, as part of the sale proceeds.
Q: Can loans be reclassified from HFS to HFI freely?
A: Transfers are at lower of cost or fair value on the transfer date; intent must be documented.

Title: Financial Services—Title Plant
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: A title insurer's plant — the indexed history of ownership and liens on local parcels — doesn't wear out if maintained; it becomes more valuable as history accumulates. So construction or purchase costs are capitalized and not depreciated, while daily maintenance is expensed.
Recognition triggers:
• Capitalize costs to construct or acquire a title plant until it can be used to issue title insurance (950-350-25).
• Expense costs of maintaining the plant and of title searches.
• Do not depreciate; test for impairment when events indicate (e.g., plant not maintained, obsolescence).
Measurement:
Basis: Cost, not depreciated
Initial: Initial: construction or purchase cost; backplant costs capitalized.
Subsequent: Subsequent: impairment only.
Journal entries: Purchase a county title plant: DR Title plant 1,500,000; CR Cash — operating 1,500,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is a title plant depreciated?
A: No — it does not diminish with use if properly maintained.
Q: Are daily updates capitalized?
A: No — maintenance costs are expensed.
Q: Why is this Topic filed under 950-350?
A: The only subtopic is Intangibles (title plant is an intangible); the source library contains 950-350.

Title: Franchisors
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: A franchisor sells the right to use its brand and system. Upfront fees usually relate to the license over the franchise term, recognized over time, unless the private-company practical expedient lets pre-opening services be a separate performance obligation. Ongoing royalties are recognized as franchisees' sales occur.
Recognition triggers:
• Initial franchise fees: generally part of the symbolic IP license recognized over the term (606); private companies may account for pre-opening services as distinct (ASU 2021-02).
• Continuing franchise fees (sales-based royalties) recognized as the franchisee's sales occur.
• Costs of continuing franchise fees expensed as incurred (952-10-25-1).
Measurement:
Basis: 606 transaction price
Initial: Allocate fees among license and distinct pre-opening services where applicable.
Subsequent: Recognize royalties when sales occur.
Journal entries: Receive an initial franchise fee: DR Cash — operating 45,000; CR Contract liability — franchise fees 45,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is the initial franchise fee earned at opening?
A: Generally no under 606 — it's recognized over the license term unless distinct pre-opening services are identified (practical expedient for private companies).
Q: How are advertising-fund contributions treated?
A: Typically as revenue of the franchisor (principal) with related expenses, unless agent considerations apply.
Q: Royalty timing?
A: As franchisee sales occur (sales-based royalty exception).

Title: Health Care Entities
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: Hospitals often know at the door that they won't collect full charges from every patient. Under ASC 606, revenue is the amount the hospital expects to collect — list prices less contractual adjustments and implicit price concessions — rather than gross charges less 'bad debt'.
Recognition triggers:
• Patient service revenue recognized under 606 at expected consideration (net of contractual adjustments, discounts and implicit price concessions).
• Charity care is not revenue; disclose cost of charity care.
• NFP health care entities also apply 958 presentation (performance indicator).
Measurement:
Basis: Expected collectible consideration (portfolio approach)
Initial: Estimate implicit price concessions using historical collections.
Subsequent: Changes due to credit events after recognition are bad debts.
Journal entries: Record patient revenue net of implicit concessions: DR Patient accounts receivable 470,000; CR Patient service revenue 470,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is bad debt on self-pay patients an expense?
A: Mostly no under 606 — expected shortfalls at inception are implicit price concessions reducing revenue.
Q: Is charity care revenue?
A: No — it's never recognized as revenue; its cost is disclosed.
Q: Portfolio approach allowed?
A: Yes, if results aren't materially different from contract-by-contract.

Title: Not-for-Profit Entities
Review notes: Technical re-read of triggers, measurement, journal entries and traps; no changes needed.
First-principles truth: A nonprofit has no owners — donors fund a mission and may restrict how their gifts are used. So equity becomes 'net assets' split by donor restriction, contributions are income when unconditional (conditional gifts wait until barriers are overcome), and the statements show how resources were used for programs versus overhead.
Recognition triggers:
• Contributions (nonreciprocal) recognized when unconditional; conditional contributions (barrier + right of return) recognized when conditions are met (958-605).
• Exchange transactions (fees for services) follow 606.
• Present net assets without donor restrictions and with donor restrictions; releases when restrictions are met.
• Present expenses by function and nature.
Measurement:
Basis: Fair value of contributions
Initial: Unconditional promises at fair value (present value for multi-year pledges).
Subsequent: Release restrictions as purpose or time is satisfied; CECL applies to exchange receivables.
Journal entries: Receive a restricted capital-campaign gift for affordable housing: DR Cash — restricted 2,000,000; CR Contributions — with donor restrictions 2,000,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is a government grant to a nonprofit a contribution or exchange?
A: If the grantor doesn't receive commensurate value, it's a contribution — often conditional (ASU 2018-08).
Q: When is a conditional pledge recognized?
A: When the barrier is overcome — not when promised.
Q: Are NFP investments at fair value?
A: Most are, with returns reported in the statement of activities.

Title: Plan Accounting—Defined Benefit Pension Plans
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: This Topic is the plan's own report (not the employer's): does the trust hold enough to pay promised benefits? It shows net assets available for benefits at fair value and the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits, so participants can judge the plan's ability to pay.
Recognition triggers:
• Statement of net assets available for benefits (investments at fair value; contracts with insurers per rules).
• Statement of changes in net assets available for benefits.
• Actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits and changes therein (960-20).
Measurement:
Basis: Fair value (assets); actuarial present value (benefits)
Initial: Plan investments at fair value (fully benefit-responsive contracts at contract value).
Subsequent: Accumulated plan benefits based on service to date.
Journal entries: Plan records employer contribution receivable: DR Employer contributions receivable 500,000; CR Employer contributions (additions to net assets) 500,000
Audit traps:
Q: Whose financial statements are these?
A: The plan's — employer accounting is ASC 715.
Q: Are future salary increases included in accumulated plan benefits?
A: No — accumulated plan benefits are based on service and compensation to date (unlike the employer's PBO).
Q: Must a plan prepare financial statements under this Topic?
A: The Topic doesn't require it (ERISA does for many plans).

Title: Plan Accounting—Defined Contribution Pension Plans
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: In a 401(k) plan, each participant owns an individual account and bears the investment risk — there is no promised benefit to measure. The plan's statements therefore show what assets are available for benefits, measured at values meaningful to participants (fair value, contract value for fully benefit-responsive contracts), and how they changed during the year.
Recognition triggers:
• Present statements of net assets available for benefits and changes therein.
• Participant loans are notes receivable at unpaid principal plus accrued interest.
• Fully benefit-responsive investment contracts at contract value.
Measurement:
Basis: Fair value (contract value for FBRICs)
Initial: Investments at fair value.
Subsequent: Remeasure each reporting date.
Journal entries: Record participant loan: DR Notes receivable from participants 20,000; CR Investments at fair value 20,000
Audit traps:
Q: Are participant loans investments?
A: No — presented as notes receivable from participants.
Q: What's contract value?
A: Measurement for fully benefit-responsive investment contracts (e.g., stable value funds).
Q: Employer vs plan accounting?
A: Employer expenses the match under 715-70; the plan reports under 962.

Title: Plan Accounting—Health and Welfare Benefit Plans
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: A health-and-welfare plan pays medical, dental and disability claims for participants. Its statements show assets available to pay benefits and the benefit obligations — including claims incurred but not yet reported — so participants and regulators see whether the plan is funded.
Recognition triggers:
• Recognize benefit obligations: claims payable, IBNR, and accumulated eligibility credits/postretirement benefit obligations (965-30).
• Present net assets available for benefits (965-20).
• Terminating plans (965-40) use the liquidation basis when applicable.
Measurement:
Basis: Fair value (assets); estimated obligations
Initial: IBNR estimated using lag studies.
Subsequent: Update each period.
Journal entries: Accrue IBNR claims: DR Benefits expense 310,000; CR Claims incurred but not reported 310,000
Audit traps:
Q: Are IBNR claims accrued by the plan?
A: Yes — they're part of benefit obligations.
Q: Employer vs plan?
A: The employer accounts for self-insured costs under 450/715-60; the plan reports under 965.
Q: VEBA assets?
A: Presented at fair value as net assets available for benefits.

Title: Real Estate—General
Review notes: Costs to rent a rental project (970-340-25-16 to 25-19, 35-2) added with a journal entry; trap corrected.
First-principles truth: Building or redeveloping property is a long manufacturing process: land, permits, construction, taxes, insurance and interest all go into producing a finished asset that will earn rent or be sold. So those costs are capitalized into the project until it's substantially complete, then allocated to units or components — while costs of simply operating or marketing the property are expensed.
Recognition triggers:
• Scope: all entities with productive activities relating to real property (970-10-15-3), except property used in non-real estate operations (970-10-15-8).
• Preacquisition costs (options, surveys, zoning, traffic studies) are capitalized if directly identifiable with the property and acquisition is probable; otherwise expensed.
• Property taxes and insurance are capitalized only while the property is undergoing development activities.
• Project costs clearly associated with acquisition, development and construction are capitalized; indirect costs capitalized only if clearly related to projects under development.
• Amenities: costs in excess of anticipated proceeds are allocated as common costs to the units benefited.
• Incidental operations: net revenue reduces capitalized costs; net costs in excess of revenue are expensed (not capitalized).
• Costs to rent a rental project (models and their furnishings, rental facilities, semipermanent signs, grand openings, unused brochures, rent-up overhead) are capitalized when related to and recoverable from future rental operations, then amortized over the period benefited; advertising follows 720-35 (970-340-25-16, 970-340-35-2 — not in the source export).
• Rental projects: capitalize costs until substantially complete and held available for occupancy (no later than one year from cessation of major construction), then expense carrying costs.
• Source note: the library contains 970-10 (overview, scope and syndication/project-cost scope); the detailed rules live in 970-340, 970-360 and 970-835, which are referenced there (970-10-15-11).
Measurement:
Basis: Historical cost, allocated by specific identification or relative value
Initial: Initial: accumulate land, hard and soft costs, capitalized interest (835-20), taxes and insurance during development.
Subsequent: Allocation to components/units: specific identification, then relative fair value (or relative sales value) methods; subsequently depreciated under 360 or relieved as sold.
Journal entries:
Capitalize property taxes during development: DR Construction in progress — real estate taxes 96,000; CR Accrued real estate taxes 96,000
Place a completed building in service: DR Buildings 38,500,000; DR Site improvements 2,100,000; DR Furniture, fixtures and equipment 1,400,000; CR Construction in progress 42,000,000
Capitalize rent-up costs of a new rental project: DR Deferred rent-up costs 50,000; CR Accounts payable 50,000
Preacquisition option cost expensed after deal falls through: DR Abandoned project costs (expense) 105,000; CR Preacquisition costs 105,000
Audit traps:
Q: Can property taxes on land held for future development with no activity be capitalized?
A: No — taxes and insurance are capitalized only while development activities are in progress; land simply held is carried without capitalizing carrying costs (they are expensed).
Q: When does capitalization stop on a rental project?
A: When the project is substantially completed and held available for occupancy — no later than one year after major construction activity ends — even if lease-up is slow.
Q: Are rent-up costs for a new building capitalized?
A: Partly. Costs to rent a rental project that relate to and are recoverable from future rental operations — model units and their furnishings, rental facilities, semipermanent signs, grand openings, unused rental brochures, rent-up overhead — are capitalized and amortized over the period benefited (970-340-25-16, 970-340-35-2); costs of current rental operations are expensed. Advertising follows 720-35. These paragraphs don't apply when the predominant rental period is under one month (970-10-15-9).
Q: How is net income from a parking lot operated on the site before development (incidental operations) treated?
A: Net incidental revenue reduces capitalized project costs; net losses are expensed — never capitalized as 'negative income'.
Q: Why can't my auditor find 970-340 in our library?
A: The source export includes only 970-10; 970-340/360/835 content is referenced by 970-10-15-11 and must be read in the full FASB Codification.

Title: Real Estate—Common Interest Realty Associations
Review notes: Technical re-read of triggers, measurement, journal entries and traps; no changes needed.
First-principles truth: An HOA collects dues from owners to run and eventually rebuild shared property — roofs, pools, elevators. It rarely owns the common areas outright in a way it could sell, so they often aren't recognized as assets; instead, the statements show operating results and the funds set aside for future major repairs, with supplementary information on the reserve study.
Recognition triggers:
• Scope: all common interest realty associations (972-10-15-2, 15-3).
• Recognize common real property as an asset only if the association has title and can dispose of it at its discretion (or it generates significant cash flows from nonmembers).
• Assessments are revenue when levied for the period; special assessments per purpose.
• Disclose funds for future major repairs and replacements and present required supplementary information from the reserve study.
Measurement:
Basis: Assessments as levied; fund accounting for replacement reserves
Initial: Initial: assessments receivable at amounts due.
Subsequent: Contract liabilities for assessments collected for future major repairs when applying 606 (practice varies after ASU 2014-09).
Journal entries: Levy monthly assessments split between operating and replacement funds: DR Assessments receivable 120,000; CR Assessment revenue — operating fund 90,000; CR Assessment revenue — replacement fund 30,000
Audit traps:
Q: Does an HOA capitalize its clubhouse?
A: Only if it holds title and can dispose of it at its discretion (or it generates significant cash flows from nonmembers); otherwise common property isn't recognized.
Q: Is the reserve-study information audited?
A: It's required supplementary information — unaudited but subject to limited procedures.
Q: Do replacement-fund assessments go to revenue immediately?
A: Under ASC 606 some associations treat them as contract liabilities until the major repair performance obligation is satisfied — a known diversity issue; follow the AICPA guide and be consistent.

Title: Real Estate—Real Estate Investment Trusts
Review notes: Technical re-read of triggers, measurement, journal entries and traps; no changes needed.
First-principles truth: A REIT is a tax-advantaged wrapper: it avoids corporate income tax if it distributes at least 90% of its taxable income and meets asset and income tests. The accounting is ordinary GAAP, but readers need to know the tax character of distributions (ordinary income, capital gain, return of capital) and how the REIT maintains its status.
Recognition triggers:
• A REIT that distributes ≥90% of taxable income (and meets other tests) is generally not subject to federal corporate income tax (974-10-05-4).
• Disclose the tax status of distributions per unit (ordinary income, capital gain, return of capital) (974-10-50-1, pending ASU 2023-06 codification of SEC rule).
• SEC Regulation S-X Rule 3-15 governs REIT presentation (974-10-S99-1); TRS income is taxable under 740.
• Equity-method and consolidation guidance for REIT JVs is referenced to 974-323/974-810 (not in this source export).
Measurement:
Basis: Standard GAAP (historical cost) — REIT status is a tax and disclosure matter
Initial: Assets measured under 360/805; income taxes only for TRSs and state taxes.
Subsequent: Distributions recognized when declared.
Journal entries: Declare a quarterly REIT dividend: DR Distributions in excess of accumulated earnings 22,500,000; CR Dividends payable 22,500,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is FFO a GAAP measure?
A: No — NAREIT FFO is a non-GAAP measure (net income excluding real estate depreciation and gains/losses on sales, plus adjustments) subject to SEC Reg G/Item 10(e) rules.
Q: Does a REIT record income tax expense?
A: For TRSs and certain state taxes, yes; REIT-level federal tax on distributed income, generally no.
Q: Why 'distributions in excess of accumulated earnings'?
A: Because depreciation makes GAAP earnings lower than cash distributions, REIT equity often shows cumulative distributions exceeding earnings.
Q: What are OP units in an UPREIT?
A: Noncontrolling interests in the operating partnership, often redeemable for REIT shares — presented as NCI (or temporary equity if cash-redeemable at the holder's option).

Title: Real Estate—Retail Land
Review notes: Placeholder 'source note' trap replaced with a collectibility trap.
First-principles truth: Retail land companies sell lots from large subdivided tracts in high volume, often with small down payments and seller financing, and promise future improvements. Historically this called for installment and deposit methods; today revenue follows ASC 606, with collectibility and the obligation to complete improvements driving timing.
Recognition triggers:
• Scope: retail land sales on a volume basis of lots from subdivided tracts (976-10-05-2).
• Revenue under ASC 606: contract existence (including collectibility of substantially all consideration) and performance obligations for promised improvements.
• Legacy 976-605 installment/deposit methods were superseded by ASU 2014-09.
Measurement:
Basis: 606 transaction price
Initial: Allocate consideration to lot and improvement obligations.
Subsequent: Recognize improvement obligations as performed.
Journal entries: Sale of a lot with an obligation to build roads: DR Cash — operating 6,000; DR Notes receivable — lot buyers 54,000; CR Land sale revenue 52,000; CR Contract liability — improvements 8,000
Audit traps:
Q: Is the installment method still used for GAAP?
A: No — superseded by ASC 606; collectibility is assessed at contract inception.
Q: How are promised improvements handled?
A: As performance obligations (or costs to fulfill) — revenue allocated to them is deferred until performed.
Q: A lot buyer pays 5% down and the developer's default rate is high. Is there a sale?
A: Only if collection of substantially all the consideration is probable (606-10-25-1). If not, no contract exists yet: cash received is a liability until the criteria are met, or until the contract is terminated and the payment is nonrefundable.

Title: Real Estate—Time-Sharing Activities
Review notes: Selling-cost trap updated for 340-40.
First-principles truth: Timeshare sellers market intervals in volume, finance most buyers and expect meaningful defaults — when buyers default, the seller recovers and resells the interval. So projects are tracked by phase, expected uncollectibility is treated as a reduction of revenue, and inventory costs are relieved using a relative sales-value method.
Recognition triggers:
• Establish and delineate a project and its phases at the outset; account for each phase separately (978-10-25-1).
• Revenue under 606 (legacy 978 profit-recognition methods superseded); estimated uncollectibility of notes receivable reduces revenue (variable consideration).
• Cost of sales and inventory using the relative sales value method, with recoveries of defaulted intervals considered.
Measurement:
Basis: Relative sales value (inventory relief)
Initial: Transaction price net of expected uncollectibility.
Subsequent: True up via cumulative adjustments to cost of sales as estimates change.
Journal entries: Sell a timeshare interval with seller financing: DR Cash — operating 3,000; DR Notes receivable — VOI 27,000; CR Vacation ownership revenue 27,300; CR Allowance — expected uncollectibility 2,700
Audit traps:
Q: Are timeshare defaults bad-debt expense?
A: No — estimated uncollectibility is a reduction of revenue under the Topic's model.
Q: How are inventory costs relieved?
A: Relative sales value method, reflecting expected recoveries of repossessed intervals.
Q: Are selling and marketing costs capitalized?
A: Commissions that are incremental to obtaining a sales contract are capitalized under 340-40 (or expensed under the one-year practical expedient); other selling and marketing costs are expensed as incurred.

Title: Regulated Operations
Review notes: Automated checks only (balanced entries, cited and in-text paragraph numbers verified against the source).
First-principles truth: When a regulator sets a utility's prices based on its costs and promises it will recover a cost through future rates, that cost is effectively a receivable from future customers — a regulatory asset — rather than an expense today. The reverse (amounts to be refunded) is a regulatory liability.
Recognition triggers:
• Apply when rates are set by a regulator, designed to recover the entity's specific costs, and it is reasonable to assume rates can be charged and collected (980-10-15-2).
• Capitalize incurred costs as regulatory assets when it is probable future revenue will recover them.
• Recognize regulatory liabilities for amounts to be refunded or future costs collected in advance.
• Discontinue 980 accounting (980-20) when criteria are no longer met; write off regulatory assets/liabilities.
Measurement:
